blocks.text: Everyone has seen an accented name turn into strange symbols, a question mark in a box, or a string of garbled characters, the infamous "mojibake" problem. This is entirely an encoding mismatch, not a data quality problem in the usual sense.

An encoding is a system for mapping human readable characters to the actual bytes stored on disk. Different encodings, like UTF-8, Latin-1 (ISO-8859-1), and Windows-1252, map the SAME byte sequence to DIFFERENT characters. Reading a file with the wrong encoding assumption produces garbled but not necessarily error raising output.
2. Why This Happens With Real Data

items: A file created on a Windows machine in one encoding gets opened assuming UTF-8, or vice versa.
Files that mix multiple encodings because they were assembled from different sources over time.

blocks.text: Attempting to read a file and getting a UnicodeDecodeError is an explicit failure signal. Garbled looking text with no error at all is a silent failure signal, both mean the wrong encoding was assumed. A library like charset-normalizer can programmatically guess the likely encoding of a raw file before you commit to reading it.

code.content:
from charset_normalizer import from_path
result = from_path('mystery_file.csv').best()
print(result.encoding)   # a best guess, e.g. 'Windows-1252'

blocks.text: A short byte string encoded and decoded with different codecs shows the exact mechanism, without needing an actual file.

code.content:
text = "café"
raw_bytes = text.encode('utf-8')

# reading UTF-8 bytes while assuming latin-1 produces garbage
garbled = raw_bytes.decode('latin-1')
print(garbled)   # "cafÃ©"

# reading them with the correct encoding recovers the original
correct = raw_bytes.decode('utf-8')
print(correct)   # "café"

pd.read_csv('data.csv', encoding='utf-8')
pd.read_csv('data.csv', encoding='latin-1')   # try if utf-8 raises a decode error
pd.read_csv('data.csv', encoding='cp1252')    # a common older Windows encoding

blocks.text: When the correct encoding is not documented, try UTF-8 first since it is the modern standard, then latin-1 or cp1252 for older Windows originated files.
6. Why UTF-8 Is the Practical Default Going Forward

UTF-8 can represent virtually every character from every language, is the modern web and systems standard, and avoids this whole class of problem for anyone downstream. When exporting cleaned data, saving it as UTF-8 is the safest default choice.
Some UTF-8 files include a byte order mark, a small invisible marker at the very start of the file. If not handled, it can show up as a strange invisible character prepended to the first column name.

code.content: pd.read_csv('data.csv', encoding='utf-8-sig')  # correctly strips a leading BOM

items: Assuming a decode error means the data itself is corrupted, when it usually just means the wrong encoding was assumed.
Silently re saving already garbled text in yet another encoding, which does not fix anything and can make the original bytes unrecoverable.
Try UTF-8 first when reading an unfamiliar file.
If a UnicodeDecodeError appears, try latin-1 or cp1252 next.
Use utf-8-sig if a strange character appears at the very start of the first column name.
Always export cleaned data as UTF-8 going forward.
Never re-save already garbled text hoping a different encoding will magically fix it.
